blind_spots.blind_spot: Safety architecture depends on GPS and ground-based radar infrastructure
blind_spots.operator_reality: A CASEVAC/blood-delivery mission under 'Logistics Under Attack' conditions is exactly where GPS gets jammed and there's no ground radar station nearby; the consumer-flight safety stack (geofences, ground radar, GPS nav) is the opposite of what a contested resupply run needs.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: The entire public safety page was written for the joyride product, which operates in fixed, permitted, uncontested US airspace near cities — the DoD cargo variant inherited that page's assumptions.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: Geofenced flight area boundaries / Ground-based radar for collision avoidance / GPS assisted navigation

blind_spots.blind_spot: Mission control model assumes a persistent voice/data link to a human controller
blind_spots.operator_reality: Their own SBIR abstract's endpoint is fully autonomous cargo drop specifically because a contested logistics run can't count on a live link back to a controller — yet their safety doctrine still centers 'Mission Control' with two-way voice as the control layer.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: The Mission Control model was built for liability/FAA-compliance reasons on the civilian joyride product, and the site hasn't been rewritten to describe how (or whether) that assumption changes for a denied-comms military drop.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: 2-way voice communication with Control ... Dedicated controllers monitoring flight telemetry

blind_spots.blind_spot: Airframe and compliance story is built entirely around FAA civilian ultralight classification, not military ruggedization or ATO
blind_spots.operator_reality: Getting the CASEVAC variant onto a program of record needs an ATO/RMF path, EMI hardening, and possibly ITAR handling for the payload system — none of which is mentioned anywhere despite the product being pitched to the Army as an operational logistics platform.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: LIFT's core identity and regulatory strategy (432lb carbon fiber, FAA Powered Ultralight, no pilot's license) was built to sell joyrides, not survive DoD accreditation, and the defense pivot is still riding on that same public narrative.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: compliant with the FAA's Powered Ultralight classification so no pilot's license is required to fly

opener_hook: Your Army contract with Near Earth Autonomy has Hexa Cargo flying 'Logistics Under Attack' missions — but the safety design on your own site (geofenced zones, ground-based radar, voice link to Mission Control) is built for the opposite: a permitted, connected joyride airspace.
what_they_do: Builds the Hexa eVTOL multirotor aircraft, primarily sold as a consumer flight experience, now adapting a cargo variant for Army uncrewed blood-delivery/CASEVAC missions under SBIR/AAL funding.
